I support the Commission's Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing and urge it to adopt the statement promptly and strengthen it.

A listed price is a promise. Consumers reasonably assume the price they see is the price others see at the same moment. Setting prices based on a company's estimate of what an individual will tolerate, using browsing history, location, device type, purchase history, or inferred income, breaks that assumption without the consumer's knowledge. It shifts value from consumers to sellers through information asymmetry, not better products or service.

As an IT professional, I can say plainly that consumers have no practical way to detect this. They cannot see the data brokers, tracking pixels, or models involved, and cannot compare their price against what others were offered. Harm that cannot be observed cannot be avoided, which is why enforcement is needed rather than reliance on market discipline.

I ask the Commission to:

Require disclosure at the point of price display, not in a privacy policy or terms of service.
Treat inferences (estimated willingness to pay, likelihood of comparison shopping, financial stress) as personal data subject to the same rules as collected data.
Guard against relabeling: a personalized price presented as a "discount," "member offer," or "loyalty price" should face scrutiny when the baseline itself is inflated by personalization.
Give special attention to essentials such as groceries, medicine, housing, and utilities, where consumers cannot easily walk away.
Scrutinize use of sensitive data (health, location, protected characteristics, and proxies for them) under the unfairness authority, not only deception.

Disclosure is a floor, not a solution. Where the Commission's authority allows, it should treat personalization of essential goods based on inferred vulnerability as unfair regardless of disclosure.

I support the FTC’s proposed policy statement and urge the Commission to enforce meaningful disclosure requirements for personalized pricing.

Consumers should not have to guess whether the price they see is the same price offered to everyone else—or whether it has been increased because an algorithm has inferred they are less likely to comparison-shop, more urgent, or more willing to pay. If a company uses a consumer’s profile, browsing behavior, purchase history, location, device, household characteristics, or data obtained from third parties to set a price, it should disclose that plainly before purchase.

Disclosure should include:

- That the price is personalized rather than broadly available.
- The principal data categories and factors used to set it.
- Whether the consumer is receiving a discount or paying more than a generally available reference price.
- The dollar amount—or, at minimum, the percentage—by which the personalized price differs from the standard price.

A vague statement such as “a specially selected price for you” is not transparency. It can conceal a penalty imposed because a business believes a consumer lacks alternatives or faces an urgent need. Consumers deserve enough information to decide whether to buy, comparison-shop, change their privacy settings, or take their business elsewhere.

Market forces cannot operate effectively when sellers have asymmetric access to personal data and can quietly charge different customers different prices for the same item at the same time. Transparent pricing supports real competition: consumers can compare offers, reward brands that price fairly, and avoid those that exploit personal data to extract more from them.

The FTC’s proposed approach appropriately recognizes that undisclosed personalized pricing can be deceptive or unfair under Section 5. My name is Narendra and I live in Austin,TX. I'm not a lawyer, and no one is paying me to write this. I pay a phone bill and an internet bill, and I've become convinced something is being done to me and my neighbors that most of us can't see and would never agree to if asked.
To be clear: I'm not talking about sales, coupons, or airfare costing more at Thanksgiving. That's dynamic pricing — it answers to the market, and everyone faces the same number. Surveillance pricing answers to me: my browsing history, my ZIP code, my device, my estimated income, whether my phone battery is low, whether I look like someone in a hurry. When the FTC studied this, it found intermediaries using everything from precise location to mouse movements to tailor prices, and that a handful of those firms served hundreds of clients.

Why this is the FCC's business. Carriers are the headwaters. Section 222 exists precisely because Congress understood we don't choose to generate this data — it's an unavoidable byproduct of using an essential service. That logic applies fully to pricing. If an inference drawn from my network data ends up in what I'm charged, the harm Section 222 was written to prevent has occurred. This isn't hypothetical: the Commission already fined all four major carriers for failing to protect subscriber location data. You've established that the pipes leak. I'm asking you to find out where the water goes.
It is regressive by design. These systems hunt for the customer who can't walk away — and because location is an input, the model knows exactly how many providers serve my address. The households with the fewest alternatives are where the algorithm can push hardest with the least risk. Rural counties. Neighborhoods that lost competitive buildout decades ago. Congress directed you to address discrimination in the terms and conditions of broadband, including on the basis of income level. Price is the term and condition.
Disclosure alone won't fix it. If my provider adds a line saying it may use my data to set prices, what have I gained? I still don't know what my price is based on, what anyone else pays, or whether I'm being overcharged — and I still can't leave. Disclosure works when it enables a choice. Where the practice is universal and the market concentrated, it just launders the practice, turning a violation into something I technically agreed to without changing a single price.
What I'm asking:
Open a Notice of Inquiry into the use of customer data to set prices and offers for communications services.
Ask carriers directly whether they use individualized data to set or vary pricing and retention offers, and what they sell to pricing intermediaries.
Confirm that using CPNI, or inferences drawn from it, to set individualized prices requires express opt-in consent — not a terms-of-service update.
Establish that a carrier cannot escape Section 222 by routing customer data through a vendor. The duty should follow the data.
Require that the price on a broadband label be uniform for everyone at a service address. A personalized label isn't a protection; it's theater.
I'll close with the part I have trouble explaining to my own family. When I say this bothers me, they say everybody has data on everybody, that ship has sailed. I feel that exhaustion too. But this is where surveillance stops being merely creepy and starts taking money out of the account. It's a decade of watching, turned around and pointed at the price tag.
What I want is simple. When I look at a price, I want it to be the price — the same one my neighbor sees, the same one a stranger sees. A fact about the product instead of a conclusion about me. We're losing that quietly, one A/B test at a time, without anyone ever voting on it. I'm asking you to notice it's being lost, and to decide on purpose whether we let it go.

Public Comment Submission
Docket ID: FTC-2026-1057

Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

Submitter: J.B. Turner / Concerned Consumer

I. The Best-Case Scenario for Personalized Pricing:
To fairly evaluate the Commission's policy proposal, we must recognize valid economic arguments supporting personalized and dynamic pricing. Advocates correctly point out that static, "one-size-fits-all" prices aren’t ideal for every market or consumer group. In theory, personalized pricing offers these advantages:

- Expanding Market Access for Price-Sensitive Consumers: Dynamic segmentation allows firms to offer targeted discounts to buyers who might otherwise be excluded due to cost. Lower initial prices enable low-income households to access goods and services like air travel and software that uniform, higher prices would restrict.

- Supporting Free and Affordable Services: Revenue from consumers willing to pay more can subsidize free or low-cost tiers accessible to the broader public. Digital platforms, open-access tools, and streaming services often use this income transfer to maintain universal access.

- Better Resource Management and Waste Reduction: Real-time adjustments promote demand shifts away from peak times (such as off-peak travel or electricity usage), helping to balance supply and prevent waste of perishable inventory like empty hotel rooms or leftover flight seats.

When transparency is upheld and savings are shared with consumers, personalized pricing can boost incivility and efficiency.

II. Market Reality: Limitations of the Model for Consumers
Despite appealing theory, real-world "surveillance pricing" practices reveal a different story. The benefits to consumers are often overshadowed by substantial harms:

- Extracting Consumer Surplus: In practice, algorithms aim not to reduce costs but to maximize willingness to pay. Instead of aiding those in need, they identify urgency or lack of alternatives, such as location or device type, to increase profits.

- The "Loyalty Penalty" Paradox: Studies show that algorithms frequently charge loyal, repeat customers higher rates, knowing they’re likely to stay, while offering cheaper prices to less loyal, deal-seeking buyers.

- Asymmetry and Deception: Unlike transparent traditional markets, algorithmic pricing depends on asymmetrical information. Merchants know details like purchase history, location, and willingness to pay, while consumers remain unaware of others’ prices for the same product.

III. Policy Recommendations for the FTC: To address the unfair exploitation of personalized pricing, I support the FTC’s stance that undisclosed, individualized prices are deceptive and unfair under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

To protect consumers without banning legitimate discounts, I recommend the FTC require:

- Clear, real-time disclosures at point-of-sale (e.g., a visible label stating: "This price is tailored to your profile or activity") rather than hidden terms.

- Explicit explanations of data factors influencing the price, such as location, browsing urgency, previous orders, or device type.

- Banning personalized price increases for urgent needs like emergency transport or essential goods during disruptions.

- Transparency and opt-in rules for data used in loyalty programs, ensuring consumers agree rather than allowing secret price hikes based on collected data.

IV. Conclusion: While personalized pricing could improve market efficiency, current practices often serve as asymmetric surveillance, eroding consumer surplus. An FTC policy demanding full price transparency will restore trust and ensure that competition, rather than covert exploitation, guides the digital economy.

Respectfully submitted.

J.B. Turner
Consumer / Citizen
Utah, USA

I am submitting this comment as a consumer who is currently homebound because of significant medical problems, and I ask the FTC to consider how personalized pricing, personalized promotions, and differences between in-store and online shopping may disproportionately affect people with disabilities, older adults, and other homebound consumers.

I have a brain tumor and POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), which causes fainting and near-fainting episodes. My physician has instructed me not to drive at this time. Grocery pickup and delivery are therefore not conveniences for me. They are currently how I access groceries.

I have been an avid coupon and sale shopper for many years. I know how to compare unit prices, shop sales, use manufacturer and store coupons, and plan meals around promotions. In the past, I could sometimes save close to $100 on a large grocery trip.

My concern is not simply that groceries cost more. I am concerned about a marketplace increasingly built around individualized offers, shopping histories, digital coupons, online product availability, and algorithms that may determine what products, prices or promotions consumers see.

When I could shop normally, if a roast was too expensive, I could compare every package in the meat case, choose a cheaper cut, look for markdowns, change my meal plan, or shop somewhere else. I cannot currently do that.

On a recent Kroger pickup order, for example, I deliberately selected a larger store farther from my home because I expected greater selection. Yet the pickup system offered me very limited meat choices, including chuck roast at $9.99/lb and stew meat at approximately $10/lb. I also encounter products designated “in-store only” or “delivery only.”

Even if an online item has the same price as that identical item inside the store, I question whether that represents meaningful price equality when a homebound consumer cannot access less-expensive alternatives, markdowns, or other choices available to an in-store shopper.

There are additional costs. I pay a monthly grocery membership fee. Delivery also means tipping, and because I live farther from the store, I feel obligated to tip appropriately for the additional distance. A 10% tip on a $300 grocery order is another $30.

I have also received dated perishable products through grocery fulfillment on multiple occasions, including products already beyond their printed date. An in-store shopper can inspect dates before purchasing. A person who cannot drive may also have difficulty returning an unacceptable item.

I am especially concerned about personalized pricing or promotions based on shopping history, location, predicted willingness to pay, likelihood of comparison shopping, or similar consumer data. A system that concludes a consumer is unlikely to comparison-shop becomes particularly concerning when the reason is that the consumer physically cannot do so.

A person with a brain tumor who has been medically prohibited from driving cannot respond to an unfavorable price by simply getting in the car and going to another grocery store.

I urge the FTC to specifically consider people with disabilities, older adults, homebound consumers, and others who depend upon digital commerce for essential goods. I strongly support the Federal Trade Commission taking a strong enforcement position against deceptive and unfair uses of personalized or “surveillance” pricing.

Consumers should be able to shop with a basic expectation that the price they see is based on the product, market conditions, and other legitimate factors—not a hidden calculation of how much an algorithm believes that particular person can be persuaded or pressured to pay.

The use of personal information such as browsing history, purchase history, location, demographics, device information, behavioral data, or other consumer-specific information to determine an individualized price creates a significant imbalance between businesses and consumers. Consumers cannot meaningfully compare prices or make informed purchasing decisions when they do not know that the price itself may have been personalized based on surveillance of their behavior.

I encourage the FTC to adopt and vigorously enforce a strong policy in this area.

In particular, the Commission should make clear that simply mentioning personalized pricing somewhere in lengthy terms of service or a privacy policy is not adequate disclosure. If personal information affects the price offered to a consumer, that fact should be disclosed clearly, conspicuously, and at the point where the price is displayed.

Consumers should also be told what categories of information materially influenced the personalized price and, where practicable, be given the ability to purchase the product or service without having their personal data used to personalize the price.

The Commission should pay particular attention to practices that exploit information suggesting urgency, vulnerability, limited alternatives, or a consumer's willingness or ability to pay more. The ability of increasingly sophisticated algorithms and artificial intelligence systems to combine large amounts of consumer data makes strong oversight increasingly important.

There is an important distinction between ordinary dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Prices changing because of supply, demand, inventory, time, or broadly applicable promotions are familiar market practices. Secretly charging or offering different prices because a business has developed a profile of an individual consumer raises fundamentally different transparency and consumer-protection concerns.

Enforcement should also address the entire ecosystem. Businesses should not be able to avoid responsibility simply because personalized prices or consumer profiles are generated by a third-party data broker, pricing platform, artificial intelligence system, or other intermediary.

Finally, I encourage the FTC to require meaningful recordkeeping and accountability. Companies using individualized pricing systems should be able to demonstrate what information their systems use, how it affects prices, what consumers are told about the practice, and what safeguards exist to prevent discriminatory, deceptive, or unfair outcomes.

Technology can make markets more efficient, but efficiency should not come at the expense of transparent pricing and informed consumer choice. Consumers should not need to use private browsing, clear cookies, conceal their location, or otherwise disguise themselves simply to determine whether they are being offered a fair price.

I encourage the Commission to adopt a strong final enforcement policy and to use its existing authority aggressively when companies secretly use consumers' personal information to manipulate the prices or offers presented to them.

To the Federal Trade Commission:

I am writing on the Commission's proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing (August 19, 2026). I support the FTC's decision to scrutinize this practice, and I urge the Commission to adopt a more assertive posture than the disclosure-only framework currently proposed.

**Personalized pricing is not a pricing strategy — it is a tax on trust.**

The traditional price tag tells every consumer, regardless of income or negotiating leverage, what a good costs. Personalized pricing replaces that shared reference point with a private calculation of "the most an individual is willing to pay," built from browsing history, location, device type, and other behavioral signals consumers never agreed to have used this way. Consumers cannot comparison-shop or even recognize when they're paying more than someone else for the same product. That isn't a market functioning efficiently — it's information asymmetry weaponized at scale.

**Disclosure alone does not fix an unequal bargain.**

The proposed statement would require disclosing that a price is personalized, its basis, and the data used. That's a step forward, but disclosure without limits does little to protect consumers. A "just tell people you're doing it" standard puts the burden of self-protection on individuals — expecting them to read fine print or use a VPN just to get a fair price. That burden falls hardest on people with less time, technical literacy, or fewer alternatives, while businesses retain every incentive to keep extracting maximum value as long as a disclosure is buried somewhere in a privacy policy.

**Personalized pricing functions as a hidden, uneven inflation.**

Personalized pricing produces invisible, individualized price increases that never show up in official price indices, because no two consumers necessarily pay the same amount for the same good. A household under financial strain — the exact household whose data may signal urgency or inelastic demand — can be quietly charged more than a wealthier household buying the identical item. This compounds real inflation by stripping away consumers' ability to seek the lowest price, one of the only tools people have when costs are already rising.

**Personalized pricing undermines the competitive foundation of capitalism itself.**

A functioning market rests on one mechanism: competition disciplines prices. When consumers can compare offers and walk away, sellers must compete on price and quality — that pressure is the only real leverage an individual has against a business with far more resources and information. Personalized pricing breaks this at the root. If every consumer sees a different, privately calculated price, there is no shared price signal left to compete against — comparison shopping becomes meaningless. That is not competition; it is each business quietly capturing maximum value from each individual, immune from ordinary market discipline. A policy limited to disclosure risks entrenching this by treating it as acceptable so long as it's labeled, rather than recognizing it as an erosion of the price competition capitalism depends on to protect consumers. Restoring transparent price competition isn't an anti-market position — it's the precondition for markets to function as intended.

**Recommendations:**
1. Use Section 5 unfairness authority to prohibit personalized pricing based on sensitive inferred data (financial vulnerability, health status, demographic proxies) — not merely require disclosure.
2. Mandate a visible, standard reference price alongside any personalized price.
3. Investigate cumulative harm to lower-income and vulnerable populations over time, not just individual transactions.

The core statutory mandate of the Federal Trade Commission is unambiguous: to protect consumers from unfair, deceptive, or anticompetitive business practices and to maintain fair, transparent market competition. 

The emergence and rapid expansion of "surveillance pricing"—the practice of harvesting detailed personal data, location metrics, browsing histories, and behavioral profiles to charge individualized, algorithmically inflated prices—directly subverts this core mission and violates the fundamental protections guaranteed under Section 5 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45).
​Surveillance Pricing Violates Section 5 Standards.

​Section 5 empowers the Commission to prohibit acts or practices that cause substantial injury to consumers which are not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition. 

Surveillance pricing fails every element of this legal standard:

​Substantial, Hidden Financial Harm: By leveraging opaque consumer profiles to extract each individual’s maximum "willingness to pay," corporations systematically strip surplus value from buyers, turning routine market transactions into predatory, asymmetrical extraction.

​Unavoidable Consumer Exploitation: Data tracking is ubiquitous across connected platforms. Because real-time dynamic pricing algorithms operate in secret, consumers cannot reasonably avoid or negotiate against individual price hikes.

​Destruction of Market Transparency: Markets depend on equal access to price signals. When two consumers viewing the exact same item at the exact same moment are offered vastly different prices based on secret algorithmic profiling, fair competition is fundamentally undermined.

​Historical Precedent: Brick-and-Mortar Price Discrimination
​The unfairness of surveillance pricing becomes undeniable when measured against established historical precedents governing physical brick-and-mortar retail:
​Congress and the FTC have long recognized the dangers of arbitrary price discrimination in physical storefronts. Enacted to curb discriminatory practices in physical retail, the Robinson-Patman Act of 1936 (15 U.S.C. § 13) established that charging different prices to different buyers for commodities of like grade and quality without cost justification damages market integrity.

 Similarly, the FTC and federal courts established clear precedent against localized predatory pricing, preventing companies from selectively manipulating prices based on geographic location to harm consumers and competitors (e.g., FTC v. Morton Salt Co., 1948).

​In a physical brick-and-mortar store, basic market fairness demands that every consumer walking down an aisle sees the exact same price posted on the shelf. If a physical retailer instructed clerks to inspect a customer's neighborhood, shopping history, or device model at the cash register and secretly mark up the price solely for that individual, it would instantly be recognized as an unconscionable, abusive trade practice. 

Digital surveillance pricing merely recreates this exact same abuse behind a screen. Corporations must not be permitted to bypass nearly a century of consumer protection precedents simply by converting physical shelf tags into algorithmic software.

​Conclusion and Requested Action
​Allowing corporate entities to weaponize personal privacy against a consumer’s wallet contradicts the foundational purpose for which the Federal Trade Commission was created. Simple disclosures or opt-out notices are entirely insufficient remedies; informing a consumer that they are being target-priced does not lessen the underlying economic coercion.

​I urge the FTC to fulfill its statutory duty, uphold its commitment to consumer protection, and exercise its full authority under Section 5 to declare data-driven surveillance pricing an unlawful and unfair trade practice.

​Respectfully, 

Concerned Consumer and solopreneur.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to surveillance pricing, the practice of using consumers' personal data to set individualized prices for goods and services.

As a Massachusetts resident who works professionally in cybersecurity, I see firsthand how much personal data is collected, aggregated, and traded without meaningful consumer awareness. Browsing history, location, device type, purchase patterns, and inferred characteristics are now being used not just to target ads, but to determine what each of us is charged. This turns the data economy against the very people it harvests from.

Surveillance pricing is fundamentally unfair. I am writing as both a consumer and a small-business attorney who regularly advises businesses regarding online transactions, disclosures, privacy, and consumer-facing practices. I strongly support the FTC's efforts to address what I believe is more accurately called surveillance pricing.

I use that term intentionally. “Personalized pricing” sounds benign, even beneficial. But when a business collects, purchases, infers, or analyzes information about an individual and uses it to determine how much that particular person may be willing to pay, the personalization is not for the consumer's benefit. It is surveillance being used to inform the (maximum projected) price presented to that consumer.

There is an important distinction between ordinary dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Consumers understand that airfare, hotels, and other products may change in price because of inventory, demand, seasonality, or timing. Those are characteristics of the market or transaction. Surveillance pricing introduces an entirely different variable: characteristics unique to the buyer.

Two consumers seeking the same product from the same seller at substantially the same time may potentially receive different prices because an algorithm predicts that one has greater ability, urgency, or willingness to pay. That creates extraordinary information asymmetry: the seller may know a tremendous amount about the consumer, while the consumer may know neither what information the seller possesses nor that it is affecting her price.

I support the Commission's proposed clear-and-conspicuous disclosure requirement, but encourage the FTC to consider whether disclosure alone is sufficient. Telling a consumer “this price has been personalized” does not tell her what the non-personalized price is, whether personalization increased her price, by how much, or whether she has any realistic way to purchase without individualized pricing.

If surveillance pricing is used, disclosure should appear at or immediately adjacent to the price—not buried in Terms of Service, privacy policies, cookie notices, or other secondary interfaces. Where feasible, consumers should also be shown the corresponding non-personalized price and whether personalization increased the price offered to them.

Consent to data collection should likewise not be treated as consent to surveillance pricing. A consumer who accepts cookies, joins a loyalty program, creates an account, or provides information necessary to complete a transaction has not necessarily made an informed choice allowing that data to be used to calculate what the seller believes she personally will tolerate paying.

I am also concerned by the suggestion that consumers can protect themselves through VPNs, private browsing, clearing cookies, changing devices, or similar measures. That places the burden backwards. Consumers should not need technological sophistication—or need to disguise themselves from a seller—to discover the market price of a product. Such a system also disproportionately disadvantages consumers who do not even know they are being profiled.

Finally, I urge the Commission to examine whether certain surveillance-pricing practices may be unfair regardless of disclosure, particularly when algorithms exploit inferred urgency, vulnerability, necessity, or lack of alternatives. A traveler responding to a family emergency, or a consumer purchasing groceries, housing, transportation, or health-related necessities, may have little practical ability to walk away. Data revealing that lack of choice should not become economic leverage against that consumer.

I therefore urge the FTC to: (1) retain and vigorously enforce clear, contemporaneous disclosure requirements; (2) require disclosure at the point the personalized price is displayed; (3) require disclosure of the non-personalized price and whether personalization increased the consumer's price; (4) distinguish clearly between market-based dynamic pricing and individualized surveillance pricing; (5) reject generalized consent to data collection as consent to surveillance pricing; (6) examine whether certain uses of surveillance pricing are unfair regardless of disclosure; and (7) clearly identify for Congress any gaps in the FTC's authority requiring legislative action.

I support the Commission's proposed policy statement on personalized pricing, and I'd ask it to go further in a few places.

When I see a price on a shelf or a website, I assume it's the same price my neighbor sees. I decide where to shop and whether to compare prices based on that assumption. If a store is quietly setting my price from data about me, I can't shop smart, because I don't know what I'm comparing. That gets worse as stores move to electronic shelf tags and app prices that can change while I'm standing in the aisle. A price has to hold still long enough for me to compare it.

Here's a specific case I'd like the Commission to address. Smart carts and scan-as-you-shop apps can tell a store what I've picked up. If I put a jar of spaghetti sauce in my cart, the store could raise the price of pasta and ground beef on my app or cart screen, because it knows I'm likely to need them and I'm already in the building. I don't know that any store does this today, but the tools exist. I'd ask the Commission to name it as unfair or deceptive, alongside its example of raising a website price when a shopper is in the store.

The bigger risk is where this could go next. Today a shelf tag, paper or digital, at least shows one price to everyone in the aisle. If stores drop shelf prices and make shoppers use an app, I'd have no way to know what the person next to me pays, and I wouldn't see my own price until I opened the app or reached the register. At that point the price can't be compared at all. I'd ask the Commission to treat removing a common posted price, in favor of app-only or checkout-only pricing, as a sign that personalization is being hidden.

I'm not against every price that varies. Surge pricing on a busy Friday night applies to everyone in the area. Insurance and loans have always been priced on the person. A loyalty discount at a store I shop at regularly is fine with me, because I know about it and it only lowers my price. My concern is a price that goes up because a company has guessed how much I'll tolerate, using data I didn't know it had.

Disclosure is the right starting point, but on its own it won't do much for most people. A line in the terms of service or a small icon near the price will be ignored, especially on a phone. I'd ask the Commission to be specific about what counts as clear and conspicuous:

1. Put the disclosure next to the price, before checkout.
2. Show the price the customer would pay without personalization, so the difference is visible.
3. Let customers see the data used to set their price and correct it, the way credit reports work today.
4. Require opt-in consent before personal data is used to raise a price.

Footnote 20 says the Commission isn't taking a position yet on whether some personalized pricing is unfair even when fully disclosed. I'd ask it to take that position for the examples it already lists: charging more because someone is having a medical emergency, traveling for a funeral, was recently the victim of a crime, or has kids at home. Those people often can't walk away from the purchase, so a disclosure doesn't protect them. Telling someone you're charging more because their situation is desperate doesn't make it fair.

If the Commission's current authority can't reach those cases, I'd ask it to tell Congress so.

Part of the Commission’s argument is that the higher price paid by consumers is unfair because the benefits to consumers and competition do not outweigh the potential for substantial injury and unavoidable issues arising from its opaqueness. They argue this is because those benefits could be conferred without concealing the fact and nature of personalized pricing. However, I believe that this argument fails to properly address the unique benefits that non-disclosure could offer, particularly when it comes to offering services at temporarily or permanently discounted prices to users in need. 
Consider this counterfactual to one of the scenarios presented as raising Section 5 concerns: If, instead of raising the price of food delivery for consumers they believe are less likely or unable to leave their homes, the delivery company chooses to lower it based on that hidden data. The company may decide to do this because they believe that the long-term profits from a reliable user outweigh those that could be gained by squeezing them for as much as possible in the short term. This trade of reduced profits for more guaranteed business shows that personalized pricing can be a win-win, but disclosure can disincentivize companies from making these offers at all. The main benefit of non-disclosure allows personalized pricing with no strings attached.
If a company is forced not only to label when personalized pricing is in effect but also to list the parameters on which it is based, it establishes consumer expectations, which can have significant consequences for the company. For example, in the food delivery scenario, the key question is how the company determines when a consumer is unlikely to leave their home frequently. Are they using GPS data? Is it based on information that correlates with certain disabilities? Is income taken into account? Is it merely the frequency of orders? Regardless, the moment they have to disclose the factors they consider when determining whether a person is eligible for a personalized price reduction will expose them to a variety of liabilities and a far higher degree of scrutiny. 
There are likely to be significant disputes from consumers who believe they meet a sufficient number of the eligibility requirements. There are also likely to be consumers who actively attempt to game those factors to get a lower price, such as leaving a phone at home all day to use GPS data, googling specific things, etc. Lastly, it also exposes them to significant criticism and public controversy over how they use their internal data to make business decisions. For all these reasons, it seems likely that the prudent decision for any business would be to avoid personalized pricing altogether. Despite the fact that it could have greatly benefited classes of people who they know would make more frequent use of their services if there was a price reduction, such as people with severe physical disabilities using delivery services. 
Even if they choose to implement these sorts of measures, there are still other issues raised by even simple disclosure. For example, to prevent disputes and scrutiny, companies may choose to rely on a single, simple data point they can cite. Imagine the food delivery company still wants to reduce prices for those who are unlikely to leave their homes. Under public scrutiny, they may require medical documentation to verify a person’s mobility issues. This would force a person to disclose more sensitive data to the company, which otherwise could have been inferred from a larger number of data points, a possibility they may avoid due to the scrutiny placed on their calculations. It would also force people to obtain clear documentation, which is a frequent difficulty for many people with disabilities, including myself. Imagine someone who is bedridden with chronic pain. Due to the often underrecognized nature of their disability, they would have a much harder time getting the kind of documentation to prove a fact that otherwise could have been inferred, and thus would be barred from a beneficial price reduction. Lastly, a company having to disclose that it uses personalized pricing creates a persistent specter of unfair price increases, even if it is only using it to lower prices to what consumers can pay. If consumers are given the option to turn it off, most would likely choose to do so despite any potential benefits; if that is not an option, they may simply avoid the business entirely, which could hurt competitive upstarts attempting to use it for growth. 
All of this is not to say that the Commission’s concerns over personalized pricing are not legitimate; they are. However, it is at the very least worth considering that there are unique benefits to the non-disclosure of these systems. Those benefits need to be considered and rebutted to make the strongest possible argument against personalized pricing.

I am deeply concerned about the growing use of personalized pricing because it represents an invasion of consumer privacy and autonomy.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether a company is examining their personal information, shopping behavior, location, browsing history, purchasing history, or other characteristics to determine the maximum price they might be willing to pay. There is a fundamental difference between a price changing because of legitimate market conditions and a company changing an individual's price because it has profiled that individual.

If personalized pricing becomes widespread, I believe it could fundamentally change the way consumers interact with businesses. Instead of making purchases directly, consumers may begin looking for ways to prevent companies from identifying them or associating their personal information with a purchase. One foreseeable response would be the increased use of proxy shoppers, intermediaries, separate accounts, or other purchasing methods designed to prevent a seller from knowing who the actual consumer is.

That outcome should be a warning sign. Consumers should not have to hide their identities or ask someone else to make ordinary purchases on their behalf simply to have confidence that they are being offered a fair price.

The burden should not be placed on consumers to become experts in privacy technology, create multiple identities, use different devices, or find proxy shoppers in order to avoid being economically penalized for information that a company has collected about them.

If a company uses personal information to determine the price offered to an individual, consumers should receive clear and meaningful disclosure before completing the transaction. They should be told that personalization is occurring, what categories of personal information are being used, and the general factors that materially affect the price.

I also encourage the FTC to consider the broader consequences of personalized pricing. Once consumers believe that revealing who they are can cause them to receive a higher price, trust between consumers and businesses can deteriorate. Consumers may reasonably respond by withholding information, avoiding loyalty programs, creating alternative accounts, using intermediaries, or otherwise attempting to prevent companies from building an accurate profile of them.

That is not a healthy direction for the marketplace.

Consumers should be able to shop as themselves without having to assume that transparency about their identity and behavior will be used against them at checkout. Personal information should not quietly become a mechanism for determining how much an individual consumer can be charged.

I urge the Federal Trade Commission to provide strong protections requiring meaningful transparency around personalized pricing and to ensure that consumers are not subjected to undisclosed price discrimination based on personal information.

I strongly support greater consumer protections against personalized pricing based on personal data.

Technology should make markets more competitive and transparent for consumers. The internet once gave consumers an extraordinary ability to compare prices and choose among competing sellers. I am concerned that increasingly sophisticated data collection and pricing technology is reversing that advantage by allowing businesses to know far more about individual consumers than consumers know about the market in which they are participating.

There is an important difference between dynamic pricing and personalized pricing. I understand that prices change because of legitimate market conditions such as supply, demand, inventory, or production costs. Personalized pricing is fundamentally different.

If two consumers attempt to purchase the same product from the same company at the same time, one should not secretly be charged more because an algorithm has determined that person is willing, able, or desperate enough to pay more.

A company may know a consumer’s location, browsing history, purchases, shopping habits, device information, or household characteristics. Meanwhile, the consumer may have no idea what other customers are paying, whether their price was personalized, what information determined it, or how to obtain the ordinary price.

That creates an unacceptable information imbalance.

I appreciate efforts to require disclosure when personalized pricing is used, but disclosure alone is insufficient. Telling consumers that their personal information is being used to determine how much they may be willing to pay does not make the practice fair.

Consumers should have meaningful control over whether their information can be used this way.

At minimum, protections should include affirmative consent before personal data is used to determine an individualized price; clear disclosure of what information influenced the price; an easy way to decline personalized pricing without losing access to the product or service; access to the ordinary non-personalized price; and strong restrictions on using sensitive information or circumstances indicating vulnerability.

Consumers should not need private browsing, VPNs, multiple devices, or other technological workarounds simply to determine whether they are receiving a fair price.

I am particularly concerned about personalized pricing for necessities or situations where consumers have limited ability to walk away. Information suggesting that someone urgently needs transportation, food, medicine, housing, security, or another essential service should never become an opportunity to extract a higher price.

This also raises a larger privacy concern. Connected technology is increasingly necessary for employment, education, banking, healthcare, transportation, communication, shopping, and ordinary participation in modern society. “Opting out” of technology is therefore becoming less realistic. Consumers should not have to surrender meaningful privacy simply to participate in the modern economy.

Healthy markets should require businesses to compete for consumers through better prices, products, service, and innovation. Technology should strengthen that competition—not become a tool for determining the maximum amount each individual can be induced to pay.

I am submitting this comment as an ordinary consumer. I am not affiliated with any company, trade group, or organization.I believe personalized pricing based on data surveillance is wrong, and that allowing it to continue unchecked puts us on a very slippery slope. But the part that alarms me most is how few people know it is happening at all.
Before writing this, I asked my husband, my family, and my friends. Not one of them knew this was going on, or that it was even possible. Every one of them assumed that the price on a website is simply the price, the same number anyone else would see. That assumption is so basic that most people have never thought to question it.
What prompted me to look into this was a video I came across in which three people in the same city pulled up the same item on target.com — a can of Spam — and were each shown a different price. The same group repeated the test on Uber, scheduling the same pickup and drop-off for the same date and time, and got wildly different fares. They tried it again booking a hotel, with the same result. Nowhere on any of those sites was there a word telling them the price they were seeing had been shaped by their own data.
That omission is the whole problem. If a retailer told me plainly that my price was personalized, I would act differently. I would comparison shop, check another device, clear my browser, look at a competitor — I would not simply accept the first number I was given. Without that disclosure, I do not know there is anything to push back against. Silence is what makes the practice work, and silence is what makes it unfair.
This hands corporations an enormous advantage over the average consumer, who has no way to detect it and no idea to look for it. And I have to ask where it ends. If companies can use these methods unrestricted and under the radar, what stops the inputs from expanding? Race. Income. Occupation. Marital status. Number of children. Age. Gender. Spending habits. These are exactly the characteristics we have decided, as a country, that people should not be treated differently on. If consumers are protected from discrimination in the workplace, why should they not have comparable protection at the point of sale?
I want to note the scale of public reaction here, because I think it speaks to the deception issue directly. Beyond my own informal polling of the people around me, the video I referenced — posted on tiktok by the account @christheproducer21 — has drawn over 16,600 comments. The overwhelming response is shock and outrage, and, more tellingly, complete unawareness that this was ever happening. When a practice can operate for years without the public having any idea of it, that is strong evidence that it defies reasonable consumer expectations.
My position is that this should not be happening at all. If you and your neighbors live in the same city and shop at the same store, the price should be the same across the board.
If the Commission concludes it cannot prohibit the practice outright, then at an absolute minimum the disclosure requirement must be real:
 1. It must appear where the price appears — on the product page, at the moment I see the number — not buried in a privacy policy or terms of service that no one reads.
 2. It must state clearly that the price is personalized, identify the categories of personal data used, and explain how that data affected the price I am being shown.
 3. It must be specific enough that an ordinary person can act on it, because a disclosure that does not let me change my behavior is not a disclosure at all.
Most people today are juggling more than enough already. They should not also have to worry that the store is quietly sizing them up. I urge the Commission to adopt the strongest possible reading of its Section 5 authority here and to enforce it aggressively.

Summary
The Commission's proposed disclosure-based framework does not merely regulate surveillance pricing — it legitimizes it. By establishing a compliance pathway (disclosure) rather than a prohibition, the FTC signals that surveillance pricing is a permissible business practice so long as procedural boxes are checked. This memo objects on two central grounds, with three supporting concerns.
Objection 1: The FTC Lacks Authority to Confer Permission Through Guidance
The FTC Act empowers the Commission to prohibit "unfair or deceptive acts or practices" — it does not empower the FTC to authorize practices that the underlying statute treats as presumptively unfair. Yet by proceeding through an informal Enforcement Policy Statement rather than formal rulemaking, the Commission avoids the notice-and-comment rigor and judicial scrutiny that would normally attach to a policy change of this magnitude, while still producing the practical effect of a rule: firms that comply with disclosure requirements gain a defensible safe harbor, and surveillance pricing becomes normalized business practice.
This is regulation by press release. An agency cannot use sub-regulatory guidance to accomplish what it lacks authority — or has not sought authority — to do through the procedures Congress and the APA require for binding rules. The disclosure framework does not merely fail to stop surveillance pricing; it affirmatively legitimizes it by giving firms a compliance checklist to follow instead of a practice to avoid. Under Loper Bright, agencies receive no deference on the scope of their own statutory authority — and the Commission should not be permitted to expand the boundaries of permissible pricing conduct through a mechanism designed to avoid that very scrutiny.
Objection 2: Surveillance Pricing Will Raise Prices Broadly, Not Just for the Wealthy
Proponents defend surveillance pricing using classical price-discrimination theory: charging high-willingness-to-pay consumers more allows firms to lower prices for low-willingness-to-pay consumers, expanding output and total welfare. That model was built on a world of static, infrequent, human-set prices and limited firm information about any individual buyer. It does not describe the current environment, in which:
Pricing is now dynamic and individualized at scale. AI-driven systems can adjust prices in real time based on granular behavioral, locational, and inferred financial data — a capability the historical economic models never contemplated and cannot reliably extend to.
The "low-end subsidy" is not guaranteed. Firms are not obligated to pass surveillance-derived margin gains to lower-income consumers as lower prices; nothing in the proposed policy requires it, and competitive pressure to do so is weak in concentrated markets.
Personalized pricing removes the disciplining function of a single posted price. A public price is a competitive signal that other firms and consumers can react to. When every consumer sees a different, privately computed price, that signal disappears — softening price competition market-wide and creating upward pressure on the effective price floor, not just the ceiling.
The practical result is more likely to be a general upward drift in prices, with the data-poor, less price-sensitive, and less tech-literate — not simply "the rich" — bearing disproportionate cost.
Supporting Concerns
Algorithmic collusion. Shared third-party pricing vendors give nominally competing firms a mechanism for tacit coordination without any explicit agreement — the "hub-and-spoke" theory DOJ has already pursued (e.g., the RealPage settlement). A disclosure-only framework does nothing to address this risk and may make such arrangements easier to defend as "compliant."
Perverse data-harvesting incentive. Personalized pricing directly monetizes the collection of consumer data, creating a financial incentive for firms to maximize surveillance — in direct tension with the FTC's own privacy enforcement mission.
Disparate impact. Pricing inputs such as zip code, device type, and browsing history function as proxies for protected characteristics. Absent affirmative safeguards, surveillance pricing risks reproducing discriminatory outcomes without requiring — or permitting easy detection of — discriminatory intent.
Conclusion
The Commission should withdraw the proposed policy statement and pursue any change to its treatment of surveillance pricing through formal rulemaking, with a presumption against — not accommodation of — data-driven individualized pricing absent a clear showing that consumer welfare is protected in practice, not merely in theory.

I am writing as an American consumer to express my strong concern about personalized pricing based on consumer data.

I understand that prices naturally change because of supply, demand, location, sales, competition, and changes in a company's costs. That is different from using information collected about an individual consumer to determine how much that particular person may be willing or able to pay.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether the person standing next to them is being offered a different price simply because an algorithm knows more about their shopping history, browsing behavior, location, purchasing habits, or other personal information.

I am especially concerned about what this could mean for ordinary working and middle-class families. The more accurately a company can determine how badly someone needs a product or how unlikely they are to shop elsewhere, the greater the opportunity becomes to extract the maximum amount that particular consumer will tolerate. That creates an enormous imbalance of information and bargaining power between businesses and consumers.

I also believe there is an important difference between offering discounts that consumers knowingly qualify for and secretly calculating individualized prices using data consumers may not even realize has been collected about them.

At a minimum, consumers should have a clear right to know when personal information is being used to determine the price or offer they receive. Consumers should also be able to purchase ordinary goods without surrendering extensive behavioral data simply to receive fair pricing.

Personally, I would prefer stronger protections that prevent retailers from using personal behavioral data to charge different consumers different base prices for the same ordinary product at the same place and time.

Technology can make a business more efficient without being used to determine the maximum amount of money that can be extracted from each individual customer.

A fair marketplace requires consumers to be able to understand the transaction they are entering. Personalized pricing based on hidden consumer profiling threatens that trust.

I write in strong support of the FTC's Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing. This policy is a meaningful step toward protecting consumers, and I urge the Commission to go further by pursuing the following additional actions within its existing authority.

Recommended Actions

- Require affirmative opt-in consent before personal data is used for pricing, not just after-the-fact disclosure. Disclosure alone allows businesses to bury notices; consent puts the consumer in control.
- Use the FTC's unfairness authority to categorically prohibit personalized pricing in high-stakes contexts where consumers cannot reasonably avoid harm, including medical transport, funeral services, emergency lodging, and food delivery in areas with limited alternatives.
- Require any business using personalized pricing to offer a standard, non-personalized price upon request. Consumers should not have to rely on VPNs or private browsing as workarounds.
- Extend FCRA-style adverse action notices to all personalized pricing. If a consumer is charged above the baseline price based on personal data, they should be entitled to know what data was used and have the right to dispute inaccuracies.
- Explicitly prohibit the use of data that functions as a proxy for race, religion, disability, or national origin in pricing models, using existing Section 5 authority and coordination with DOJ and HUD.
- Require large platforms to file annual reports under Section 6(b) disclosing what data categories feed pricing models, the resulting price variance, and demographic breakdowns of who pays more.
- Pursue a trade regulation rule under Magnuson-Moss that establishes per-violation civil penalties for undisclosed personalized pricing, giving enforcement real deterrent power beyond case-by-case action.

Disclosure is a floor, not a ceiling. American consumers deserve pricing protections that match the sophistication of the data systems being used against them. I urge the Commission to use every tool available to it to make that a reality.

I strongly support meaningful consumer protections against undisclosed personalized or “surveillance” pricing.

I understand that prices legitimately change because of supply and demand, inventory, timing, geography, promotions, and other normal market factors. My concern is something very different: a company using information collected about me—such as my browsing history, purchasing history, location, device information, demographics, previous interactions, or other personal data—to determine how much it believes I personally am willing to pay.

Two consumers looking at the same product or service at the same time should not unknowingly be quoted different prices simply because an algorithm has concluded that one of them can or will pay more.

This creates an enormous information imbalance. Companies can know a great deal about an individual consumer, while the consumer may know virtually nothing about how the price being displayed was determined. That undermines meaningful comparison shopping and makes it impossible to know whether you are seeing a generally available market price or a price specifically engineered for you.

At a minimum, if a business uses personal information to determine or influence the price shown to an individual consumer, that practice should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously before the purchase. Consumers should be told what categories of personal information are being used and should have a meaningful opportunity to opt out and receive a price that is not based on their personal profile.

I also believe there is an important distinction between dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Consumers understand that an airline seat, hotel room, concert ticket, or other product can change in price as market conditions change. What consumers should not have to accept is a hidden system in which the price changes because a company has profiled the particular person asking for it.

The ability to collect increasingly detailed information about consumers should not become an invisible mechanism for determining how much more each individual can be persuaded to pay.

I urge the FTC to establish strong transparency requirements and to aggressively enforce existing consumer-protection laws when personalized pricing practices are deceptive or unfair. Consumers deserve to know when their personal information is affecting the price they are being offered.

Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement on Personalized Pricing
I'm submitting this comment as an independent commercial food broker and business owner. I manage wholesale pricing, retail markups, and supply chain logistics in the retail grocery sector. I know the mechanics of how goods are priced from the manufacturer to the checkout counter.
The FTC’s proposal to mandate disclosure for surveillance pricing fails to solve the core problem. Disclosures shift the regulatory burden directly onto consumers. Shoppers don't have the time, technical data, or market leverage to decipher complex algorithmic pricing models before buying necessities. Relying on fine-print disclosures doesn't protect consumers; it gives corporations a legal shield to continue exploiting private data.
While the retail grocery sector relies on tight margins and visible competition, broad digital commerce currently operates in a black box. Retailers use personalized data—browsing history, device type, geographic location—to dynamically inflate prices for targeted individuals. This practice fundamentally distorts fair market competition. It creates massive information asymmetry where the retailer holds every advantage over the individual buyer.
The FTC must aggressively classify algorithmic personalized pricing as an "unfair and deceptive practice" under Section 5 of the FTC Act. You don't need to wait for a new statutory ban to act. When a digital platform alters a price based on a user's hidden digital profile, rendering them incapable of accessing the baseline market rate, the practice is inherently deceptive.
Stop treating surveillance pricing as a transparency issue. It is a structural market abuse. I urge the Commission to apply Section 5 and penalize the specific algorithmic tactics corporations use to penalize consumers.

I support the FTC's scrutiny of personalized pricing, but I am concerned that the proposed policy places too much weight on disclosure without establishing whether consumers actually have a reasonable means of avoiding the resulting injury.

Section 5(n) of the FTC Act requires consideration of whether consumer injury is “reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.” I believe the final policy should address that question much more directly.

If a company tells me that my price was personalized using my data, what exactly am I able to do about it?

The proposal does not appear to guarantee that I can reject personalization and receive a non-personalized price. Shopping elsewhere may not solve the problem either. Multiple retailers may share corporate ownership, use the same or overlapping data brokers or pricing intermediaries, or otherwise have access to substantially the same profile. Avoiding one retailer therefore does not necessarily allow the consumer to escape the information producing the personalized price.

There is also a fundamental problem with the profile itself. I may have no practical ability to see it, challenge it, or know whether its inferences actually describe me. A household account illustrates the problem. My spouse may make purchases through an account associated with me. The underlying transaction history can be completely accurate while the conclusion that it represents my preferences, behavior, or willingness to pay is completely wrong.

More fundamentally, personalized pricing alters the informational balance of a transaction. A seller traditionally knows its costs, margins, and minimum acceptable price while the consumer knows his or her own maximum willingness to pay. Neither side knows the other's reservation price. Surveillance-based personalized pricing potentially allows the seller to retain its own private negotiating information while using data collected about the consumer to estimate the consumer's maximum price.

The consumer has no equivalent visibility into the seller's negotiating position.

I also question whether the Commission can presume that consumers voluntarily expose themselves to this system simply by participating in modern commerce. Avoiding the generation of digital behavioral and transactional data can require substantial withdrawal from ordinary online and increasingly data-dependent commerce. The fact that avoidance is technically possible does not necessarily mean that the resulting injury is “reasonably avoidable” within the meaning of Section 5(n).

For these reasons, I ask the Commission to address several questions explicitly in the final policy:

What meaningful mechanism allows a consumer to reject personalized pricing and obtain a non-personalized price?
How is injury “reasonably avoidable” when the consumer's underlying profile can follow the consumer across nominally competing sellers?
What ability does a consumer have to inspect, challenge, correct, or reject not merely inaccurate raw data, but inaccurate attribution and inferences drawn from accurate data?
How will the Commission evaluate situations in which avoiding personalized pricing requires significant search costs, privacy measures, technological knowledge, or withdrawal from ordinary digital commerce?
Does disclosure alone make an otherwise unavoidable injury reasonably avoidable?

I am not asking the Commission to prohibit conduct beyond its statutory authority. I am asking it to address an apparent gap within the proposed policy's own Section 5 framework.

Disclosure gives a consumer information. It does not necessarily give the consumer agency.

If the consumer cannot reject the personalized price, cannot obtain a neutral price, cannot reasonably escape the profile by changing sellers, and cannot meaningfully challenge the profile being used, I do not understand how disclosure alone makes the resulting injury reasonably avoidable.

I urge the Commission to address that distinction explicitly before finalizing this policy.

Price discrimination, although perhaps unpleasant to the ear of some, is a long-recognized economic tool observed in in any robust retail market. Price discrimination is a basic form of personalized pricing that allows sellers to offer discounts to customers who are otherwise less likely to purchase while still maintaining a price above the marginal cost of production. A coupon (whether targeted or made available all), a rebate, even a weekly sale are all forms of price discrimination, often discriminating in favor of the buyer willing to make the extra effort to utilize the discount.

The Commission errs when it seeks to restrict the actions of free actors in the market based on what the Commission decides consumers reasonably expect. The long-established norm the Commission must recognize is that sellers may use any legally obtained information to set prices in their best interest, and buyers may and should be encouraged to do the same. The Commission may encourage consumers to take economic classes, but they must not require sellers to teach them at every checkout opportunity. The example provided in section III, in which the Commission indicates a straightforward indication of personalized pricing would be insufficient because does not contain an unspecified amount of information, suggests the Commission intends to apply a standard to online purchases not currently applied to the price discrimination examples given above.

The Commission should not shape the future of commerce. Governments do consumers no favors by seeking to restrict prices or commerce in general. The Commission must not seek to prohibit personalized pricing of any sort without highly specific evidence of significant harm that outweighs a benefit to the overall market. I oppose the proposed statement as drafted.
The Commission acknowledges that Congress has not authorized a ban on personalized pricing. A policy statement should not create a new three-part disclosure duty and then declare that noncompliance is “likely” an unfair or deceptive practice that the agency will enforce aggressively. That is rulemaking without rulemaking: it chills lawful conduct, imposes primary obligations, and skips the findings and cost-benefit analysis a trade rule would require.
The liability trigger is too vague. “Where consumers reasonably expect that prices will not vary based on their personal data” does not tell a business when ordinary variation—by time, inventory, channel, membership, coupon, location, or device—becomes “personalized pricing.” A standard that uncertain produces selective enforcement, not clearer markets.
The disclosure regime is overbroad. It does not cleanly separate targeted discounts, loyalty prices, and personalized offers from concealed markups. Treating those practices as one category will put dense notices on programs that lower prices for many shoppers, or cause firms to drop the offers rather than try to describe “willingness to pay” and “types of data” at checkout. A short notice risks being called misleading; a complete notice is unreadable and may expose proprietary methods. That is not a workable compliance path.
The economics do not support a presumption of harm. The welfare effects of price discrimination are ambiguous. Personalized pricing often expands sales to price-sensitive customers. In competitive markets, quietly charging someone above the going price loses the sale. If the practical result of this statement is fewer targeted discounts and one higher uniform price, the shoppers the policy claims to protect will be worse off.
Extreme examples—funeral travel, medical emergencies, crime victimization—do not justify a market-wide disclosure code for routine algorithmic merchandising. If those practices occur and are concealed, existing Section 5 already reaches material deception and unfair injury. The Commission does not need a new presumption that any undisclosed use of personal data in pricing is likely unlawful.
The Commission should withdraw or sharply narrow the statement. At minimum, any final version should:
state that it creates no independent legal duty;
exclude loyalty programs, coupons, membership prices, and other reductions from a disclosed list or public price;
drop the presumption that non-disclosure is “likely” a Section 5 violation;
require case-specific proof of a material misrepresentation or omission; and
avoid compelling firms to label ordinary pricing as an estimate of a consumer’s willingness to pay.
Respectfully submitted,
Concerned Consumer 
Massapequa, NY
